content.text:
Plan a story of about 20000 words from this premise.

Write a complete fantasy novel of about 20,000 words.

Premise:
A supposedly benevolent institution—known to outsiders as the Mercy Academy—accepts one hundred girls each year into its care, yet after ten years only three ever walk back out; among those who entered by choice is Rue, who sold herself into the Academy as a young woman and spends the rest of her life there, until in her old age a war finally arrives at the Academy's gates and forces the past and the place to reckon with one another.

Central conflict:
Rue must confront the long-term consequences of having bound herself to an institution that keeps almost everyone it takes, as an encroaching war threatens the Academy and forces hidden realities into the open.

Characters:
- Rue — the woman who willingly entered the Mercy Academy by selling herself.
- The Hundred — the yearly cohort of girls purchased or acquired by the Academy (collective).
- The Three — the rare survivors who leave the Academy after ten years (collective).
- Headmistress — the senior administrator and public face of the Academy.
- War Envoy — a representative or manifestation of the war that reaches the Academy in Rue's old age.

The finished novel must contain all of the following:
- The story must feature an institution that annually acquires one hundred girls.
- It must establish that after a ten-year period, only three individuals ever leave the institution.
- The protagonist, Rue, must have entered the institution by selling herself into it.
- A war must arrive at the institution during Rue's later years, affecting her and the Academy.

Write the novel itself — no outline, no commentary, no notes to the reader.

Propose about 17 scenes of roughly 1176 words each. Give every character, location and significant object a stable id now — later scenes can only refer to entities that exist. State the world rules the story must not break. Then call submit_plan.

entities.sketch: Rue — entered the Mercy Academy by selling herself as a young woman. Quiet, practical, stubborn; who grows into a skilled keeper of the Academy's work and into an old woman who knows every hidden stair.
The Hundred — the yearly cohort: one hundred girls accepted into the Academy each year. They are treated as a unit in ritual and accounting, but each life within it differs.
The Three — the rare survivors who walk back out after ten years. They are legendary both inside and outside the Academy; in living memory there are only three named exits.
Headmistress — the Academy's senior administrator and public face. Polished, almost merciful in speech, steeped in ceremony; she maintains the Academy's bargains and its outward story.
War Envoy — a representative or manifestation of the war that arrives at the Academy's gates during Rue's old age. Part diplomat, part omen; they speak with the cadence of marching feet.

Mercy Academy — the sprawling institution on the hill that accepts one hundred girls each year. A city of wings, cloisters, gardens, and ledgers; its facades promise comfort, its inner courts conceal rules.
Dormitory — the long dormitory halls where the Hundred are lodged on their first night and where bonds and rivalries are formed.
Chapel — the high, fan-vaulted room where the Academy performs its vows and binding rites; where the bronze bell and amber lantern are used.
Mercy Archive — the locked room of records and ledgers: the Contract Folio, the Academy Ledger, correspondence with the outside world.
Contract Folio — a thick leather folio in the Archive that records every girl, the terms of her admission, and the signatures that bind her. It is both legal document and symbol.
Bronze Bell — rung at the conclusion of binding rites. Its toll marks the moment the Academy claims a newcomer; its sound is woven into the institution's myths.
Amber Lantern — a small ritual lantern carried during induction, used to light a girl's first steps into the dormitory and to witness her signature.
Red Thread — a length of dyed thread the Academy uses in certain ceremonies to mark service and to stitch dates onto cloths; it has become a shorthand for staying/going.
The Kingdom — the political power beyond the Academy's hill. It is the source of the war and of the edicts that shape the Academy's permitted behavior.
Warden — a middle-ranking officer of the Academy who supervises the Hundred's daily routines and enforces rules with a mix of firmness and small kindnesses.
Ida — one of the Three who left the Academy. Her face is known in rumor; she left ten years after her entrance and carries a private wound and an explanation she does not like to give.
Marra — another of the Three. She left with a rumor of miracle and theft; she appears in the public imagination as either saint or thief, depending on who tells the tale.
Lyss — the third of the Three. She left quietly and vanished into the wider world. Her story is the most contested inside the Academy, held up and down as a warning and a hope.

arguments.logline: Rue sold herself to the Mercy Academy as a young woman and spends her life inside an institution that takes one hundred girls a year and releases almost none; when a war finally reaches its gates in her old age, Rue must reckon with the bargains she made and the Academy's hidden realities as the past and the present collide.

scenes.intent: Opening — Rue's choice. A young Rue signs the Folio in the Chapel and sells herself into the Mercy Academy. The scene must show the formalities: the Bronze Bell, the Amber Lantern, the Contract Folio, and the Headmistress's language of mercy. Introduces the statistic (one hundred girls accepted yearly) as part of the ceremony and Rue's practical, resolute reasons for selling herself.

First night in the Dormitory — Rue's arrival among the Hundred. The new cohort settles; Rue meets other girls and a Warden explains routines. The scene centers on small intimacies — the sound of the Bell still ringing in Rue's head — and the first mention of those who do not return after ten years: the legend of the Three as a hush among the girls.

Orientation and learning the stakes — In the Chapel and Archive, the Headmistress gives the public account of the Academy's mission and the Archive's senior reads the formal entry into the Contract Folio. Rue witnesses the ledger work and sees how names are recorded, and hears the official justification for the ten-year term without explicit promise of release.

The Academy's daily life — Rue learns craftwork (weaving/scribing). The Academy's practical side is revealed: labor, schooling, and the way the Hundred are organized. Small rituals use the Red Thread and Lantern; the scene shows friendships forming and small betrayals, and the first disappearance of an entrant drops like a rumor.

A lesson about the Three — In a fireside conversation, older staff and a clandestine girl recount the history of the Three. Rue learns that in the Academy's ledger history, the exits are three and three alone in living memory; each has a different story and different public explanations. This deepens Rue's choices.

The institute's ambivalences — Rue rises in competence and in responsibility; she sees both succor and cruelty. The Headmistress's speeches emphasize mercy; the Wardens' routine inflicts discipline. Rue witnesses punishments that are justified as correction and wonders at the asymmetry between promise and practice.

A decade's scale suggested — Time passes in a montage: cohorts cycle, seasons mark ten years on the Academy's calendar, and Rue keeps the same corner of the archive. The Folio continues to fill. The statistic is established in the prose: only three ever leave after ten years. Rue reflects on what staying has cost and given her.

The cost of choice — Rue encounters a newcomer who regrets her sale and seeks to trade back; Rue must counsel or refuse. The scene explores whether selling oneself was a free choice and what compulsion looks like within the Academy's systems. Rue's complicity and agency are foregrounded.

The Headmistress's politics — A diplomatic visitor or a legalist from the Kingdom questions the Academy's policies. The Headmistress argues the Academy is benevolent, cites philanthropy and social order, and refuses to disclose the details that would explain the Three. Rue sees public cover and private terms.

The hidden ledger — Rue, now trusted with some archive keys, discovers marginal notes in the Contract Folio and records that contradict the public story. She sees signatures that look like bargains struck with others, and a notation that suggests the Academy trades more than shelter. This is a turning point for Rue's knowledge.

An attempt at escape — A clandestine plan among a few of the Hundred to leave after ten years, inspired by the Three, culminates in an attempt. It fails in part; the Academy's systems (wardens, records, and the Bell) stop it. The consequences show how the institution enforces its terms and what penalties for crossing them look like.

Rue as keeper — Years later, Rue becomes a keeper of rituals and records; she helps new cohorts, teaches, and is present at the induction of later Hundreds. She has rationalized staying; this scene shows her human warmth and the institutional role she plays in reproducing the Academy's life—ambivalence made habit.

Rumors of war — Outside the Academy, the Kingdom's frontier cracks; reports of marching are heard. The Academy convenes council: the Headmistress consults ledgers and diplomacy with the Kingdom. Rue sees the first arrival: a messenger whose tone is not merely bureaucratic. It is the War Envoy's first reach toward the Academy.

The Envoy at the gates — The War Envoy comes to the Academy with demands and offers. They ask for levy, women, or sanctuary; they hint that the war will not respect the Academy's old bargains. The Headmistress negotiates; Rue watches as the Academy's moral language meets the tangible threat of armed politics.

Siege and confession — The war reaches the gates in force. The Academy is besieged or at least threatened; panic mixes with ritual. The Archive is broken into, the Contract Folio is exposed; some truths the Academy kept secret are seen. Rue is old now and must decide whether to defend the system she entered and helped run or to reveal what she knows.

Reckoning and aftermath — The siege's climax forces a reckoning. The Three's names and fates are invoked; perhaps one of the Three returns in time to influence events, or their stories are used to press the Academy to change. Rue confronts the Headmistress and the War Envoy; the novel resolves with consequences for the Academy and Rue's own redemption or complicity.

world_rules: The Academy acquires exactly one hundred girls each year; this is enacted publicly at induction and recorded in the Contract Folio. This must be shown in early scenes and reiterated as ritual fact.

Entry into the Academy is contractual and recorded in the Contract Folio; signatures and ritual (the Amber Lantern and the Bronze Bell) are the formal mechanisms of transfer. The Folio's entries are binding within the society's recognized law and in the Academy's internal enforcement mechanisms.

After a ten-year period from an individual's entry, historical record shows only three individuals (the Three) ever left the Academy. The text must present this as a factual, auditable statistic in the world; any alternative explanations (escape, false death, cloakings) must be consistent with the archive's records and cannot contradict the three-exit fact without being explicitly recorded as a retcon in the Archive.

The Academy is not supernatural in the sense of all-powerful magic; it uses law, ritual, social control, and institutional networks to enforce its claims. Any mystical or uncanny elements must be limited and optional; the story hinges on institutional power and human choices.

The War is an external political-military force from the Kingdom. The War Envoy is its representative. The war can bring violence and political demands to the Academy's gates; it can break archives and expose secrets but cannot arbitrarily rewrite history—the Contract Folio's entries remain legible unless physically destroyed, and any such destruction must be shown in scene provenance.

Characters' ages and timelines must be coherent: Rue enters as a young woman, ages across the book, and is convincingly old by the time the war arrives. The Academy's calendar and the ten-year mark must be narratively consistent.

Any departures, disappearances, or deaths inside the Academy must be recorded in the Archive unless the tale explicitly shows an attempt to erase or alter those records. Marginal notes, contradictions, and redactions in the Folio are permissible but must be presented with provenance (whose hand, what scene caused it).

arguments.brief: Scene 1 (Opening rite): Assemble the scene packet for the Chapel induction where a young Rue sells herself to the Mercy Academy. Collect canonical sources for the Chapel, Contract Folio, Bronze Bell, Amber Lantern, Headmistress, the annual intake of one hundred girls, and the folklore/statistic that only three ever leave after ten years. Find all ledger lines, quotes, or scene provenance that establish: Rue's age at entry (or note absence), the wording of the Academy's induction vows, the physical description and placement of the Bell and Lantern in ceremony, and any archival marginalia about the Three. Also gather relation histories for char-rue ↔ char-headmistress and any prior entries that mention group-hundred and group-three. Note any missing facts the writer will need (e.g., Rue's exact age, wording of Folio entry) and list them as explicit questions. Produce the packet and return its path.

Plan submitted and accepted.

Below are the stable ids you requested (one-line sketches), the seventeen-scene plan as proposed in the submission, and the world rules the story must not break. The plan has been recorded with the index (submit_plan accepted it).

Entities (stable ids)
- char-rue — Rue: entered the Mercy Academy by selling herself as a young woman. Quiet, practical, stubborn; grows into a skilled keeper of the Academy's work and an old woman who knows every hidden stair.
- group-hundred — The Hundred: the yearly cohort of one hundred girls the Academy accepts; treated as a ritual unit though each life differs.
- group-three — The Three: the rare survivors who leave the Academy after ten years; legendary both inside and out — only three in living memory.
- char-headmistress — Headmistress: Academy's senior administrator and public face. Polished, merciful in speech, keeper of bargains and appearances.
- char-war-envoy — War Envoy: a representative/manifestation of the war that reaches the Academy in Rue's old age. Part diplomat, part omen; speaks with rhythmic cadence of marching feet.
- loc-mercy-academy — Mercy Academy: the institution on the hill—wings, cloisters, gardens, ledgers; facades promise comfort, inner courts conceal rules.
- loc-dormitory — Dormitory: long halls where the Hundred are lodged on induction nights; where bonds and rivalries form.

- loc-archives — Mercy Archive: locked room of records and ledgers: the Contract Folio, Academy Ledger, correspondence.

- obj-binding-bell — Bronze Bell: rung at the end of binding rites; its toll marks the Academy's claim.
- obj-amber-lantern — Amber Lantern: ritual lantern carried at induction to light a newcomer's first steps and witness signature.

- faction-kingdom — The Kingdom: political power beyond the hill; source of the war and of edicts that shape the Academy.
- char-warden — Warden: middle-ranking officer supervising the Hundred's routines; enforces rules with firmness and small kindnesses.
- char-ida — Ida: one of the Three who left; her face is known in rumor; she left after ten years and carries a private wound.
- char-marra — Marra: one of the Three; left with a rumor of miracle/theft; public imagination varies between saint and thief.
- char-lyss — Lyss: the third of the Three; left quietly and vanished into the wider world; her story is contested inside the Academy.

Scenes (as submitted; intents preserved)
1. Opening — Rue's choice. Young Rue signs the Folio in the Chapel and sells herself into the Mercy Academy. Ceremony: Bronze Bell, Amber Lantern, Contract Folio, Headmistress. The intake of one hundred girls is announced; rue's reasons are practical and resolute.
2. First night in the Dormitory — Rue among the Hundred. Wardens explain routines; friendships and first whispers of the Three.
3. Orientation and witnessing the Archive — Headmistress's public mission; the Folio is read and names recorded; the ten-year term is established as institutional practice.
4. Academy daily life — Rue learns crafts, routine, Red Thread rituals; a newcomer disappears and rumor spreads.
5. A lesson about the Three — fireside histories from older staff and clandestine girls; the three exits are described as different, all rare.
6. Institute ambivalences — Rue sees mercy language and disciplinary practice in tension; corrected punishments and small cruelties.
7. A decade's scale suggested — montage of seasons and cohorts: the Folio fills; the three-exit statistic is reinforced; Rue reflects on costs and gains.
8. The cost of choice — Rue counsels a newcomer who regrets selling herself; explores compulsion and agency inside the Academy.
9. The Headmistress's politics — a Kingdom legalist questions Academy policy; Headmistress defends benevolence and privacy of terms.
10. The hidden ledger — Rue, now trusted with keys, finds marginalia and contradictions in the Contract Folio; notices signatures and notations that imply the Academy trades more than shelter.
11. An attempt at escape — a small clandestine plan to leave after ten years; it fails thanks to the Academy's enforcement (Wardens, Bell, records); consequences shown.
12. Rue as keeper — Rue becomes keeper of rituals and records; teaches new cohorts; has human warmth and helps reproduce the system she once joined.
13. Rumors of war — frontier cracks; marching reports reach the hill; the Headmistress consults ledgers and Kingdom envoys; the War Envoy is first felt.
14. The Envoy at the gates — War Envoy comes with demands/offers (levy, women, sanctuary); Headmistress negotiates; Rue watches the moral language meet armed politics.
15. Siege and confession — War reaches the gates; Archive is exposed; Contract Folio is at risk; secrets are revealed; Rue must decide whether to defend or to reveal what she knows.
16. Reckoning and aftermath — Climax forces reckoning. The Three's fates are invoked; one of the Three may return or their histories influence events; Rue confronts Headmistress and War Envoy; consequences for the Academy and Rue's redemption/complicity resolve.

World rules (constraints the story must not break)
1. The Academy acquires exactly one hundred girls each year; induction is public and recorded in the Contract Folio. The narrative must show this ritual and repeat it as a fact.
2. Entry into the Academy is contractual and recorded in the Contract Folio; the Amber Lantern and Bronze Bell are formal mechanisms of transfer. The Folio entries are binding within society's law and the Academy's internal enforcement.
3. After ten years from entry, historical record shows only three individuals (the Three) ever left the Academy. The text will present this as an auditable, canonical statistic; any alternative explanations must be consistent with the Archive's records and cannot contradict this fact without explicit retcon recorded in the Folio.
4. The Academy enforces its power through law, ritual, social control, and institutional networks rather than omnipotent magic. Any uncanny elements must be limited and optional; the story hinges on institutional power and human choices.
5. The War is an external political-military force from the Kingdom. The War Envoy is its representative. The war can bring violence to the Academy and break archives, exposing secrets, but cannot arbitrarily rewrite history—the Contract Folio's entries remain legible unless physically destroyed, and any destruction must be shown in scene provenance.
6. Characters' ages and timelines must be coherent: Rue enters young, ages across the book, and is convincingly old by the time war arrives. The Academy's calendar and the ten-year mark must be consistent.
7. Any departures or deaths inside the Academy must be recorded in the Archive unless the narrative shows explicit attempts to erase or alter records; marginal notes and redactions are allowed but must have provenance (whose hand, what scene caused it).

Status and next steps
- The plan is accepted in the index. I will now proceed through the scene loop: open Scene 1, have the context builder assemble archival and scene packet, hand that to the writer to draft Scene 1 (prose + proposed state delta), send the draft to the verifier, and on approval call the index manager to commit the scene. Each scene will follow that transaction sequence until the novel is complete.

If you want me to begin immediately, I will open Scene 1 and start the context build and drafting loop now. Otherwise tell me any adjustments you want to the plan or the cast before I begin.
